Synthesis of Multisubstituted 2,3-Allenamides via Palladium-
Catalyzed Carbonylation of Propargylic Esters

ABSTRACT: 2,3-Allenamides are an important class of unsatu-
rated group-substituted carbonyl compounds. A palladium-
catalyzed aminocarbonylation of propargyl acetates with amines
for the synthesized tri-/tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenamides has been
developed. A broad range of tri-/tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenamides
have been prepared from propargyl acetates in good to excellent
yields. The reaction featured mild reaction conditions and good
functional group tolerance. The applicability of this methodology was further highlighted by the late-stage modification of several
natural products and pharmaceuticals.
■
INTRODUCTION
2,3-Allenamides are an important class of unsaturated group-
substituted carbonyl compounds.
1
This type of structure exists
in natural products, medicinal chemistry, and agrochemical
industry (Figure 1).
2
For example, allenamide compound III
was used to selectively label target cysteine residues in fully
unprotected peptides and proteins.
2c
Compound IV was
reported to inhibit T790M/L858R double mutant and wild
type EGFR kinases in a low nanomolar range.
2
In addition, 2,3-
allenamides also serve as versatile building blocks in organic
synthesis due to their unique structure and reactivity. With a
unique orthogonal cumulative π-system, this structure has been
widely used in a range of transformations, such as cyclization
reactions,
3
nucleophilic and radical addition reactions,
4
and
cycloaddition reactions.
5
Traditional methods for the synthesis of allenoates and 2,3-
allenoic acids is based on a Wittig-type reaction,
6
which usually
yielded a mixture of allenoates and alkynoates. Direct
carboxylation reaction of allenylmetal reagents with carbon
dioxide was also reported,
7
but this method requires
preparation of organometallic reagents and suffers from poor
functional group tolerance. Many other strategies have also
been developed for the synthesis of allenyl ketones or
allenoates, such as transition metal catalyzed β-H elimination
of enol triflates
8
and 1,4-difunctionalization of enyne
compounds.
9
Although there are many synthetic studies on
allenoic acids, allenoic ketones, and allenoates, there are only
limited reports on the synthesis of 2,3-allenamides.
On the contrary, the transition-metal-catalyzed carbon-
ylation reaction has become one of the most powerful tools
for the synthesis of carbonyl compounds.
10
The carboxylation
of the readily available propargylic alcohols and their
derivatives with CO provides an efficient way for synthesis of
2,3-allenoic compounds.
11
Marshall reported the synthesis of
trisubstituted 2,3-allenamide compounds from propargyl
methanesulfonate. The reaction requires high CO pressure to
achieve good selectivity; otherwise, a large amount of
propargyl amines will be produced (Scheme 1a).
12
In 2014,
Bi and co-workers reported a silver-catalyzed cross-coupling of
propargylic alcohols with isocyanides for the synthesis of di/

13
However, only
two primary isocyanides were reported to undergo clean
conversion. The direct carbonylation of propargyl alcohol
derivatives and secondary aliphatic amine feedstocks to
synthesize 2,3-allenamides is rare.
14
Thus, the development
of a general and effective method for the synthesis of 2,3-
allenamides is still highly desirable.
With a continuous interest in the reactions involving
propargyl alcohol and the carbonylation reaction,
15
we herein
report a palladium-catalyzed aminocarbonylation of propargyl
acetates with amines for the synthesize tri-/tetrasubstituted
2,3-allenamides (Scheme 1c). The main features of this
reaction include the following: (1) preparation of tri-/
tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenamides with propargyl acetates under
mild reaction conditions, (2) broad substrate scopes (including
some natural products and pharmaceutical intermediates) as
well as good functional group tolerance, and (3) efficient
catalysis with low catalyst loading.

Finally, we examined the effect of the ligands (entries 13−16).
Bidentate ligands were less effective in this reaction (entry 14,
and see details in Supporting Information (SI)). Among the
monodentate ligands, dpppy has a good effect on the reaction
(entry 16, 91%).
With the optimal reaction conditions in hand, the scope of
the method was examined. As shown in Scheme 2, a variety of
propargyl acetates bearing electron-neutral, electron-rich, and
electron-deficient aryl moieties underwent this transformation
smoothly, forming tri-/tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenamides. A
variety of functional groups, including OMe, SMe, Me, Ph,
OAc, F, Cl, and Br, on the aromatic ring of the substrates were
all well tolerated (3aa−3ja, 67−92%), with the halogen moiety
acting as a potential synthetic handle for subsequent
modification (3ha−3ja). It was noted that the steric hindrance
has an influence on the reactivity: the high steric hindrance was
detrimental to the reactivity (3aa, 91% vs 3ca, 67%). Products
with electron-donating and -withdrawing groups (3aa−3ja,
66−92%) can be successfully prepared. Notably, 4-(1-acetoxy-
3-phenylprop-2-yn-1-yl)phenyl acetate (1g) was suitable for
this reaction and gave allenamide 3ga (66%). Several useful
aromatic functionalities, such as pyrene-1-yl (1k), 2,3-
dihydrobenzofuran-5-yl (1l), furan-2-yl (1m), and benzo[b]-
thiophene-3-yl (1n), accommodated the aminocarbonylation
furnishing 3ka−3na in 82−89% yields. Then, we attempted to
synthesize tetrasubstituted allenamide compounds (3oa−3sa)
via tertiary propargyl acetates (Scheme 2). The results show

were efficiently converted to 3oa−3sa in good to excellent
yields (79−93%), and it is noteworthy that terminal cyclic
tertiary propargyl acetate 1s was tolerated to furnish product

derived from (−)-myrtenal. The intermediates of canagliflozin
and empagliflozin can be successfully synthesized into their
derivatives 3za−3Aa (75−78%) and compound 3Ba (84%)
derived from the natural product estrone.
Finally, we expanded the scope of amine compounds using
1-(4-methoxyphenyl)-3-phenylprop-2-yn-1-yl acetate (Scheme
3). We found that a variety of secondary amines are suitable for
this reaction. Common drug fragments such as thiomorpho-
line, piperazine, and piperidine can be reacted smoothly, and
the products 3ab−3ad are obtained in excellent yields (86−
90%). The ketal compound 4-piperidone vinyl ketal can
successfully prepare compound 3ae (87%). Acyclic amine 2e
containing amide and ester structures can react smoothly to
obtain compound 3af (81%). We also prepared some drug
derivatives based on drugs or drug fragments. The donepezil
derivative 3ag (82%) can be obtained by using debenzyldo-
nepezil. Desloratadine and amoxapine can also be used directly
to synthesize drug derivatives 3ah (82%) and 3ai (77%). In
addition, we investigated the reactivity of the aniline
compounds in this reaction. When N-methylaniline was used
to react under standard reaction conditions, the target
compound 3aj could be obtained in moderate yield (56%).
Based on our research and previous related work,
14b
we
proposed a possible mechanism (Scheme 4). Taking the
generation of 3aa as an example, the initially situ-generated
active Pd(0) species performs ligand exchange with propargyl
alcohol 1a acetate to give the precursor A, which affords
allenylic palladium intermediate B through oxidative addition.
Subsequently, coordination and migratary insertion of CO
formed acylpalladium intermediate C. Next, ligand exchange of
acetate with amine in the presence of base generated
intermediate D, which undergoes reductive elimination to
give product 3aa. Meanwhile, Pd(II) is converted to Pd(0) and
participates in the next catalytic cycle.

■
CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed a novel palladium-catalyzed
aminocarbonylation of propargyl acetates for the one-step
synthesis of 2,3-allenamide compounds. The transformation
uses easily available substrates to efficiently deliver a broad
range of multisubstituted 2,3-allenamides under mild con-
ditions and low pressures of CO. This protocol exhibits broad
substrate scope as well as good functional group tolerance and
facile capacity of modification of natural products and
pharmaceuticals.
■
